newsitem.title: DENMARK: Denmark's tobacco-loving queen marks jubilee. [CORRECTED 16:53 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Denmark's tobacco-loving queen marks jubilee. [CORRECTED 16:53 GMT]

text.p: Denmark's Queen Margrethe II, who celebrates 25 years on Europe's oldest throne (corrects to insert dropped word "oldest") on January 14, has made newspaper headlines lately because of a storm over Swedish criticism of her public smoking.

Rarely seen in public without an ashtray at her elbow, she drew criticism from Gothenburg newspaper columnist Hagge Geigert last weekend in an article slamming the Danish monarch for setting a bad example by lighting up in public places.

Geigert said the queen "puffed away freely" during a visit to asthmatic residents of an old people's home and he compared her unfavourably to Swedish King Carl XVI Gustaf, who also smokes but only in private.
The Swedish offensive unleashed a tidal wave of outrage and Copenhagen newspapers covered their front pages with indignant headlines.
"Smoke War against the Swedes", "Let the Queen Smoke in Peace", "Mind your own business, Sweden" and "Keep up the puffing, Margrethe" were only a few.
"Is it a sign of responsibility for the Swedish king to slink off to the toilets to have a drag on the sly?", the tabloid Ekstra Bladet asked.
Asked during a November news conference to comment on her "smoking problem" the queen's response was terse.
"I have no problem," she said.
The tobacco-loving queen, known to intimates as Daisy, has other claims to fame than her nicotine habit.
Due to a 1953 amendment to the right of succession to include royal daughters, she became the first woman to sit on the 1,012-year-old Danish throne since the first Margrete became ruler in 1353.
Margrethe II is a capable artist who has designed sets and costumes for television and the Royal Ballet and has illustrated a Danish edition of J.R.R. Tolkien's "Lord of the Rings".
Educated at two Danish universities and the Sorbonne in Paris as well as Cambridge and the London School of Economics in Britain, she once described herself as an eternal student.
A second cousin to Britain's Queen Elizabeth, she is also related, through the Greek royal family, to Prince Philip and is kin to the royal houses of Norway, Sweden and Spain.
Margrethe became queen at the age of 31 on January 14, 1972 when her father King Frederik IX died after a two-week illness.

The eldest of three daughters, she was born in Copenhagen on April 16, 1940, one week after the wartime German invasion of Denmark. The national flags put out nationwide at her birth served also as a gesture of defiance toward Nazi occupation and the royal baby became a symbol of hope for the future.
In 1963, while studying at the Sorbonne, the tall blonde princess met French Count Henri de Laborde de Monpezat.
Their relationship developed during the following year in London, where the 30-year-old count was posted as third secretary at the French embassy.
They married on June 10, 1967 and King Frederik created his son-in-law Prince Henrik of Denmark.
Their first son, Fredrik, was born in May 1968 and followed by a second boy, Joachim, in June the following year.
Crown Prince Frederik is unlikely to become king for many years, as his 56-year-old mother says she will never step down.

"It's never been a tradition in this country to abdicate, you are duty-bound to carry on for life. I feel myself that one is duty-bound to go on to the end," she told the November news conference, drawing rueful agreement from Prince Henrik.
"Of course it would be very pleasant to have a wife who has more time for her husband, but I don't see this happening," he said.
